---
title: "Two-part models"
subtitle: "Expected outcomes from a model of whether the outcome is positive and a model of how large it is"
---
<<dd_version: 2>>

Outcomes such as medical expenditures are zero for many people and spread over
a long right tail for the rest. A two-part model handles them in two steps: a
binary model of whether the outcome is positive, and a model of its size for
the people with a positive outcome. The expected outcome is the product of the
two:

$$E(y) = \Pr(y > 0) \times E(y \mid y > 0)$$

This is the model the `twopm` command fits (Belotti, Deb, Manning, and Norton
2015). With `suest2`, fit the two parts as separate models, combine them, and
give `margins` the product of the two predictions in `expression()`. Each
`predict()` names its model with `model()`, so the same combined results also
give effects within each part, comparisons across groups, and comparisons
across two-part models.

The examples use the medical expenditures of 19,386 adults in the 2004 Medical
Expenditure Panel Survey.

## Fit the two parts and combine them

The first part is a logit of whether a person had any medical expenditures.
The second part is a `glm` with a gamma family and a log link, fit to the
people who had any. Both cluster on the dwelling unit (`duid`).

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
use "https://tdmize.github.io/data/data/meps", clear
generate byte any = exp_tot > 0
tabulate any

local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

quietly logit any `x', vce(cluster duid)
estimates store Any

quietly glm exp_tot `x' if any, family(gamma) link(log) vce(cluster duid)
estimates store Amount

suest2 Any Amount
<</dd_do>>
```

## Expected expenditures and effects on them

`predict(model(Any))` is the probability of any expenditures and
`predict(model(Amount))` the expected expenditures of someone who has any.
Their product is the expected expenditures:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local twopart "predict(model(Any)) * predict(model(Amount))"

margins, expression(`twopart')
margins, dydx(age female ins_unins anylim) expression(`twopart')
<</dd_do>>
```

Expected expenditures average about $3,760 a year. Being uninsured lowers them
by about $2,610, and each year of age raises them by about $63.

## Effects in each part

Naming one model in `predict()` gives the effect in that part alone:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
margins, dydx(ins_unins) predict(model(Any))
margins, dydx(ins_unins) predict(model(Amount))
<</dd_do>>
```

Being uninsured lowers the probability of any expenditures by 24 percentage
points, and the expected expenditures of someone who has any by about $2,480.
Both are averaged over the whole sample.

## Comparing groups

`over()` gives the effect within each group, and `over(r.)` the difference
between the groups, with its test:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local twopart "predict(model(Any)) * predict(model(Amount))"

margins, dydx(ins_unins) over(female) expression(`twopart')
margins, dydx(ins_unins) over(r.female) expression(`twopart')
<</dd_do>>
```

Being uninsured lowers expected expenditures by about $2,170 for men and $2,980
for women; the difference, about $810, is significant.

## Other models for the second part

**A linear second part.** Fit `regress` among the people with any
expenditures, and use its prediction in place of the `glm` one:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

quietly regress exp_tot `x' if any, vce(cluster duid)
estimates store Linear

quietly suest2 Any Linear
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(predict(model(Any)) * predict(model(Linear)))
<</dd_do>>
```

**A regression of log expenditures.** When the second part is a regression of
the log of the outcome, its prediction is on the log scale. Exponentiating it
gives exp(*xb*), which understates the mean; the expected outcome is exp(*xb*)
times the mean of the exponentiated errors. Two estimates of that constant are
common: Duan's (1983) smearing estimate, the mean of the exponentiated
residuals, and, if the errors are normal, exp(*s*²/2), where *s*² is the
residual variance. Compute either one from the stored regression and include
it in `expression()`:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

generate double lnexp = ln(exp_tot) if any
quietly regress lnexp `x' if any, vce(cluster duid)
estimates store LnAmount
local s2 = e(rss) / e(N)

predict double res if e(sample), residuals
generate double expres = exp(res)
summarize expres, meanonly
local duan = r(mean)

display "Smearing constant: " %5.3f `duan' _n "Normal constant:   " %5.3f exp(`s2' / 2)

quietly suest2 Any LnAmount
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(predict(model(Any)) * exp(predict(model(LnAmount))) * `duan')
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(predict(model(Any)) * exp(predict(model(LnAmount)) + `s2' / 2))
<</dd_do>>
```

`margins` treats the constant as known, so the standard errors do not include
the uncertainty in estimating it.

## Weights and survey data

**Sampling weights.** Fit each part with the weights but without `vce()`, and
give the clustering to `suest2` with `cluster()`:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

quietly logit any `x' [pw = wtdper]
estimates store AnyW

quietly glm exp_tot `x' if any [pw = wtdper], family(gamma) link(log)
estimates store AmountW

quietly suest2 AnyW AmountW, cluster(duid)
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(predict(model(AnyW)) * predict(model(AmountW)))
<</dd_do>>
```

**Survey data.** `svyset` the data and fit each part with `svy:`. Fit the
second part with `if any`, as above, not with `subpop()`; `suest2` computes the
standard errors from the full survey design.

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local x "c.age i.female c.lninc c.pcs12 c.mcs12 i.ins_unins i.anylim"

svyset duid [pw = wtdper]

quietly svy: logit any `x'
estimates store AnyS

quietly svy: glm exp_tot `x' if any, family(gamma) link(log)
estimates store AmountS

quietly suest2 AnyS AmountS
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(predict(model(AnyS)) * predict(model(AmountS)))
<</dd_do>>
```

## Comparing two two-part models

`suest2` can combine more than one two-part model. Here a two-part model
without the health measures (`pcs12`, `mcs12`, and `anylim`) is combined with
the full one, to ask how much the effect of being uninsured changes when health
is held constant. The difference between the two expected outcomes goes in one
`expression()`:

```{.stata-run}
<<dd_do>>
local x1 "c.age i.female c.lninc i.ins_unins"

quietly logit any `x1', vce(cluster duid)
estimates store Any1

quietly glm exp_tot `x1' if any, family(gamma) link(log) vce(cluster duid)
estimates store Amount1

quietly suest2 Any1 Amount1 Any Amount

local tp1 "predict(model(Any1)) * predict(model(Amount1))"
local tp2 "predict(model(Any)) * predict(model(Amount))"

margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(`tp1')
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(`tp2')
margins, dydx(ins_unins) expression(`tp1' - `tp2')
<</dd_do>>
```

Without the health measures, being uninsured lowers expected expenditures by
about $2,840; with them, by about $2,610. The difference, about $230, is
significant.

## References

> Belotti, Federico, Partha Deb, Willard G. Manning, and Edward C. Norton.
> 2015. "twopm: Two-part Models." *Stata Journal* 15(1): 3--20.
> <https://doi.org/10.1177/1536867X1501500102>

> Duan, Naihua. 1983. "Smearing Estimate: A Nonparametric Retransformation
> Method." *Journal of the American Statistical Association* 78(383):
> 605--610. <https://doi.org/10.2307/2288126>
